narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Being in the second decile, well below the average of roughly sixth decile among accepted students, signaled that you struggled to keep pace with your peers later in the program. This had the largest impact on the outcome.

Your undergraduate GPA came next in importance, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.20 it sits only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, giving the model a modest reason to expect you might still pass. Unfortunately this positive signal was not strong enough to outweigh the other factors.

Your first-year class ranking added a smaller additional push toward failure. Like your third-year rank, a second-decile placement is noticeably lower than the sixth-decile average among those who were admitted.

Taken together, the model saw your later-year academic standing as the dominant concern. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your study habits and academic performance now, perhaps by seeking tutoring or adjusting your course load, then retake the LSAT or reapply once you have clearer evidence of consistent high performance.
